# The Unix Shell {#sec-shell} The HF-HOME case report form (CRF) export arrives from the data manager, and before loading it into R you ask the shell two quick questions. Is the header where you expect it? `grep -c '^patient_id' crf_export.csv` counts the lines that begin with the first column's name and answers 0. How many patients have no discharge weight, which two of the sites record as an empty last field? `grep -c ',$' crf_export.csv` also answers 0. The true answers are 1 and 9: the file begins with three invisible bytes, a byte-order mark (BOM), and every line ends in a carriage return that the terminal does not display. Nothing failed; the shell answered exactly the questions you typed, about a file that is not quite the one on your screen. This chapter teaches the working subset of the shell, and the habit of looking at the bytes before you trust a count. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *This is the Unix philosophy: Write programs that do one thing and do it well. Write programs to work together.* [Doug McIlroy]{.smallcaps}, quoted in Peter H. Salus, *A Quarter Century of UNIX* (1994) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: the shell belongs to the Environment band, the layer from which Git, R, Quarto, and Docker are all run.](04b-shell_files/figure-pdf/fig-shell-pipeline-1.pdf){#fig-shell-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Environment.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 20 minutes. **You'll need.** A terminal running `bash` or `zsh`: Terminal on macOS, any terminal on Linux, and on Windows either Git Bash (installed with Git for Windows) or WSL, the Windows Subsystem for Linux; @sec-workstation covers both. The HF-HOME files in `analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/` of the book's repository, whose `README.md` is the codebook. The shell commands run from `analysis/report/`, the directory this book is built in. The R verification steps use: ```r library(readr) library(dplyr) ``` **You'll be able to.** - Move around the filesystem and write the relative path to a data file from any working directory. - Find a file's row count, delimiter, byte-order mark, and line endings before R reads it, and confirm the count in R. - Build a pipeline from `cut`, `sort`, `uniq`, and `grep` that answers a counting question, and translate it to `dplyr`. - Write a short script with `set -euo pipefail` that checks a directory of raw files without modifying them. **Outline.** - [Navigating the filesystem](#sec-shell-navigate) - [Looking at a file before R does](#sec-shell-inspect) - [Pipes and redirection](#sec-shell-pipes) - [Searching with grep and find](#sec-shell-search) - [Worked example: a script that checks the raw files](#sec-shell-worked) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-04b. 1. What does the pipe operator `|` do in the shell, and how does it resemble the R pipe `|>`? 2. What is the difference between an absolute path and a relative path, and what do `.`, `..`, `~`, and `/` refer to? 3. Why might you write a short shell script to run an analysis pipeline rather than clicking through the steps by hand each time? ::: ## Navigating the filesystem {#sec-shell-navigate} The shell is a text interface to the operating system. You type a command, the shell runs a program, and the program prints its output. Its power derives from a design decision made in the early 1970s: build many small programs, each doing one thing well, and let the output of one become the input of the next. You can go far in data science without the shell, but not without friction, because the tools this book depends on (Git, Docker, `ssh`, and the schedulers of a computing cluster) are all operated from it. The chapter uses `bash`, the default on most Linux systems and inside almost every Docker container; macOS ships `zsh`, which differs only in details that do not matter here. Three commands answer 'where am I, what is here, and how do I move' (display-only, because the output is your machine's): ```bash pwd # print working directory (where am I?) ls # list files here ls -la # long listing, including hidden files cd ~/research/trial # change directory (absolute path from home) cd .. # up one level cd - # back to the previous directory ``` Every command in this chapter that shows output was run from `analysis/report/`, so a path to the HF-HOME files climbs one level and descends two: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code} ls ../data/raw_data/hfhome #> baseline.csv #> crf_export.csv #> demographics.csv #> labs.csv #> medications.csv #> outcomes.csv #> randomization.csv #> README.md #> visits.csv ``` ::: Paths come in two kinds. An *absolute* path starts from the root of the filesystem and names the full location, such as `/home/user/data/visits.csv`. A *relative* path starts from where you are, such as `data/visits.csv`. A path that begins with `/` or `~` is absolute; anything else is relative to the working directory. | Symbol | Means | Example | |---|---|---| | `/` | The root of the filesystem | `/usr/bin/env` | | `~` | Your home directory | `~/research/trial` | | `.` | The current directory | `./check-raw.sh` | | `..` | The parent of the current directory | `../data/raw_data/hfhome` | : Path shorthands. {#tbl-shell-paths} ### Exercises 1. From the repository root (the directory that contains `analysis/`), what relative path reaches `visits.csv`? From `analysis/report/`? Check each with `ls`. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} From the root, `analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/visits.csv`; from `analysis/report/`, `../data/raw_data/hfhome/visits.csv`. `ls` on the path prints the path back if the file exists and `No such file or directory` if it does not. The same file has a different relative path from each directory, which is why a script that uses relative paths must also say which directory it runs from. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A colleague's script begins `read_csv("data/visits.csv")` and works for them. It fails for you with 'does not exist', although the file is in the repository. What is the likeliest cause? **Answer.** The path is relative, so it is resolved from the working directory, and you ran the script from a different directory than your colleague did (for example from `analysis/` rather than the repository root). Run `pwd`, or `getwd()` in R, to see where you are. The durable fix is a convention the whole project follows, such as always running from the root, or the `here` package, which builds paths from the project root wherever the script is run. ::: ## Looking at a file before R does {#sec-shell-inspect} A malformed or enormous file can choke R if you read it blind, and a subtly malformed one can be read without complaint into the wrong values. A few seconds at the shell tell you the row count, the delimiter, and whether the bytes are what they appear to be, before R ever sees the file. | Command | Answers | |---|---| | `head -n 5 file.csv` | What do the first lines look like? Is the delimiter a comma? | | `tail -n 5 file.csv` | Does the file end cleanly, or with a footer or a half-written line? | | `wc -l file.csv` | How many lines (newline characters)? | | `tail -n +2 file.csv` \| `wc -l` | How many lines after the header? | | `head -c 16 file.csv` \| `od -c` | What are the first bytes, including invisible ones? | | `head -n 2 file.csv` \| `cat -e` | How does each line end? (`$` is the newline, `^M` a carriage return) | | `less file.csv` | Page through the file; `q` quits | : Triage for a data file. {#tbl-shell-triage} ### The visible file ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code} cd ../data/raw_data/hfhome head -n 3 crf_export.csv wc -l crf_export.csv tail -n +2 crf_export.csv | wc -l #> ﻿patient_id,site,sex,dob,discharge_date,ef_pct,sbp_discharge,weight_kg #> 0001,Site B,Female,1946-10-11,2024-02-01,66,154,71.8 #> 2,Site E,F,19460328,20240201,55,159,64 #> 2433 crf_export.csv #> 2432 ``` ::: The header names eight columns separated by commas, as the CSV (comma-separated values) format prescribes, and the two data rows already show two of the sites' conventions: one writes sex as `Female` and dates with dashes, the other `F` and dates as eight digits with the identifier's leading zeros gone. `wc -l` counts newline characters, so the second count, which skips the header, is the number of data rows if no quoted field contains a line break. ### The invisible bytes The two questions from the opening, asked as typed: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code} cd ../data/raw_data/hfhome grep -c '^patient_id' crf_export.csv || true grep -c ',$' crf_export.csv || true #> 0 #> 0 ``` ::: `grep -c` exits with an error status when it counts zero matches, and `|| true` keeps that status from stopping a script; the zeros are the misleading answers. `head` shows characters as your terminal draws them, and a terminal draws neither a BOM nor a carriage return. Two commands show the bytes themselves: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code} cd ../data/raw_data/hfhome head -c 16 crf_export.csv | od -c head -n 2 crf_export.csv | cat -e #> 0000000 357 273 277 p a t i e n t _ i d , s i #> 0000020 #> ﻿patient_id,site,sex,dob,discharge_date,ef_pct,sbp_discharge,weight_kg^M$ #> 0001,Site B,Female,1946-10-11,2024-02-01,66,154,71.8^M$ ``` ::: `od -c` prints each byte, and the first three, `357 273 277` in octal (`EF BB BF` in hexadecimal), are the UTF-8 byte-order mark, a marker some Windows tools write at the start of a file. `cat -e` marks the end of each line with `$`, and the `^M` before it is a carriage return: the file has Windows (CRLF, carriage return and line feed) line endings, 2,433 carriage returns in 2,433 lines. This is why the two `grep` counts in the opening returned 0: no line begins with `patient_id`, because the first begins with the BOM, and no line ends in a comma, because every line ends in `\r`.[^file-cmd] [^file-cmd]: The `file` command is often recommended for this triage, and versions without a test for CSV files report both the BOM and the CRLF line terminators. Versions that recognize CSV files (`file` 5.41 on the macOS machine that built this book, for one) report only `CSV text` and say nothing about either; `file -e csv crf_export.csv` turns the CSV test off and restores the full report. Minimal Docker images often lack `file` altogether, while `od` and `cat` are always present. `readr` strips the BOM and accepts either line ending, so R is not fooled by this file. The verification below is the one to run on every count you take at the shell. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Count the data rows at the shell and in R, and require that the two agree: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(readr) shell_rows <- system2("bash", c("-c", shQuote( "tail -n +2 ../data/raw_data/hfhome/crf_export.csv | wc -l" )), stdout = TRUE) crf <- read_csv(crf_path, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), na = character()) stopifnot(as.integer(shell_rows) == nrow(crf)) nrow(crf) #> [1] 2432 names(crf)[1] #> [1] "patient_id" ``` ::: The counts agree, and `readr` has removed the BOM from the first column's name. When they disagree, a quoted field holds a line break, or the last line has no final newline; find out which before you trust either number. ::: ### Copying, moving, and deleting The commands that change files are short, and two of them cannot be undone (display-only): ```bash mkdir -p data/derived # make a directory, and its parents cp a.csv b.csv # copy mv a.csv archive/ # move or rename rm scratch.csv # delete: no trash can, no undo ``` `rm` does not move a file to a trash can; it deletes it, and `rm -rf` on the wrong directory is unrecoverable. Read a deletion command before running it, and never build one from a variable you have not inspected. A redirection that writes to a file you are also reading is the quieter version of the same mistake. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code} tmp=$(mktemp -d) cp ../data/raw_data/hfhome/crf_export.csv "$tmp/crf.csv" wc -c < "$tmp/crf.csv" tr -d '\r' < "$tmp/crf.csv" > "$tmp/crf.csv" wc -c < "$tmp/crf.csv" rm -r "$tmp" #> 120573 #> 0 ``` ::: The chunk works on a copy in a temporary directory and deletes the directory at the end; the second count shows what happened to the copy. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **Redirecting a command's output onto its own input empties the file.** The shell opens `crf.csv` for writing, which truncates it to zero bytes, before `tr` reads a single byte, so the command reads an empty file and writes an empty file, and reports no error. On a raw export this destroys the evidence (Habit 2). Write the repaired version somewhere else, for example `tr -d '\r' < crf_export.csv > ../derived/crf_lf.csv`, and never point a redirection at a file in the raw-data directory. ::: ### Exercises 2. Using only the shell, find the number of data rows, the delimiter, and the column names of `visits.csv`. Does it carry a BOM? Does it have CRLF line endings? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} visits_path <- file.path(hf_dir, "visits.csv") visits <- read_csv(visits_path, show_col_types = FALSE) nrow(visits) #> [1] 6317 names(visits) #> [1] "visit_id" "patient_id" "visit_type" "visit_day" "visit_date" visits_bytes <- readBin(visits_path, "raw", file.size(visits_path)) visits_bytes[1:3] #> [1] 22 76 69 sum(visits_bytes == as.raw(0x0d)) #> [1] 0 ``` ::: `tail -n +2 visits.csv | wc -l` prints the row count above, `head -n 1 visits.csv` shows the comma-separated, quoted column names, `head -c 16 visits.csv | od -c` begins with `"` rather than `357 273 277` (no BOM), and `head -n 2 visits.csv | cat -e` shows lines ending in `$` with no `^M` (no carriage returns, as the zero count above confirms). Of the HF-HOME files, only the CRF export carries either. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** `wc -l` reports 2,433 lines for a CSV file with a header. Can you conclude that it holds 2,432 records? **Answer.** Not yet. `wc -l` counts newline characters. A quoted field that contains a line break (a free-text comment, say) adds a line without adding a record, and a last line with no final newline is a record that `wc -l` does not count. The shell count is a fast first estimate; the record count is what a CSV parser reports, which is why the Verification compares the two rather than trusting either. ::: ## Pipes and redirection {#sec-shell-pipes} The pipe `|` connects the output of one command to the input of the next, as R's `|>` connects functions. Redirection sends output to a file with `>` (overwrite) or `>>` (append), and reads input from a file with `<`. @fig-shell-pipe traces the HF-HOME laboratory file through a five-stage pipeline. Each stage does one thing, and the data narrow at every step, which is the whole design. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-shell-pipe %%| fig-alt: "Left-to-right pipeline. labs.csv, one line per test %%| result, feeds tail -n +2, which drops the header; then cut, %%| which keeps the third field; then sort, which makes duplicates %%| adjacent; then uniq -c, which counts runs; then sort -rn, which %%| ranks the counts. The output is one line per test code." %%| fig-cap: "A shell pipeline as a sequence of narrowing %%| transformations. Each tool reads standard input and writes %%| standard output, so composition needs no shared file format %%| beyond lines of text. This is the compositional idea of a %%| dplyr pipeline in a different notation." flowchart LR F["labs.csv
one line per result"] F --> H["tail -n +2
drop the header"] H --> A["cut -d, -f3
keep one field"] A --> B["sort
make duplicates adjacent"] B --> C["uniq -c
count runs"] C --> D["sort -rn
rank"] D --> G["one line per test
the answer"] ``` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code} cd ../data/raw_data/hfhome tail -n +2 labs.csv | cut -d, -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn #> 6319 "K" #> 6318 "CREAT" #> 4082 "NTPROBNP" #> 4081 "SODIUM" #> 2433 "HGB" ``` ::: The line reads as a sentence: drop the header, keep the third comma-delimited field, sort it, count each distinct value, and rank the counts. `uniq -c` counts *adjacent* repeats, which is why the first `sort` is required. The quotation marks are part of the field, because `cut` knows nothing about CSV quoting; a field that contains a quoted comma would be split in the wrong place, which is one reason to keep the shell for questions and R for analysis. ### The shell and R side by side Every pipeline in this chapter has an R equivalent, and the equivalent is the check. The shell is excellent glue (fetching files, orchestrating steps, inspecting inputs) and a poor place to do statistics: draw the line where @sec-wrangling draws it, and do the analysis in R. | Question | Shell | R | |---|---|---| | First rows | `head -n 5 f.csv` | `head(df, 5)` | | Number of records | `tail -n +2 f.csv` \| `wc -l` | `nrow(df)` | | Rows matching a pattern | `grep -c 'Site E' f.csv` | `sum(stringr::str_detect(df$site, "Site E"))` | | One column | `cut -d, -f2 f.csv` | `select(df, site)` | | Count of each value | `cut -d, -f2 f.csv` \| `sort` \| `uniq -c` | `count(df, site)` | | Distinct values | `cut -d, -f2 f.csv` \| `sort -u` | `distinct(df, site)` | : The same questions at the shell and in R. The shell versions read lines and split on every comma; the R versions read records and respect quoting. {#tbl-shell-vs-r} ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Repeat the laboratory count in R: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "labs.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |> count(test_code, sort = TRUE) #> # A tibble: 5 x 2 #> test_code n #> #> 1 K 6319 #> 2 CREAT 6318 #> 3 NTPROBNP 4082 #> 4 SODIUM 4081 #> 5 HGB 2433 ``` ::: The counts should match the shell's line for line. ::: ### Repairing line endings without touching the raw file The pipe also repairs the opening's count. `tr -d '\r'` deletes every carriage return on its way through, and the file on disk is not changed: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code} cd ../data/raw_data/hfhome tr -d '\r' < crf_export.csv | grep -c ',$' tail -n +2 crf_export.csv | tr -d '\r' | grep -c ',$' #> 9 #> 9 ``` ::: The first count is the opening's 9, and the second confirms that the header is not among them. To keep the repaired version, redirect it to a file outside the raw-data directory, as the Pitfall above requires. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} A model writes shell pipelines fluently, and the error it makes is the field number or an invisible byte, not the syntax. > **Context.** I have a CSV file. Its header, and two lines of the > file passed through `cat -e`, are below [paste them; for real > patient data, paste the header and one invented row, never real > rows]. I want the number of records for each value of the > `site` column. > > **Constraints.** Use only `head`, `tail`, `cut`, `tr`, `sort`, > `uniq`, and `grep`, with options that work in both the macOS > (BSD) and GNU versions. Read the file; do not write to it or to > its directory. > > **Criteria.** Before the pipeline, state the field number you > chose and why, and whether the file has a header, a BOM, or CRLF > endings, citing the `cat -e` output. After it, give the > `dplyr` code that should produce the same counts. *Failure mode.* The model counts fields from zero or from the wrong end, drops the `sort` before `uniq -c`, or ignores the `^M` that `cat -e` shows, so that every count is plausible and one category is split in two. *Check.* Run both the pipeline and the `dplyr` code and compare them line for line, as in the Verification above. A header and an invented row are structure, not data, so they may go to any approved tool (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ### Exercises 3. How many distinct spellings of the site label does `crf_export.csv` contain? How many sites remain after you convert to lower case and remove leading and trailing spaces? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} At the shell: ```bash cd ../data/raw_data/hfhome tail -n +2 crf_export.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq | wc -l tail -n +2 crf_export.csv | cut -d, -f2 | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]' | sed 's/^ *//; s/ *$//' | sort | uniq | wc -l ``` The first count is 25 and the second 5, computed here in R from the same bytes: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} length(unique(crf_site)) #> [1] 25 length(unique(tolower(trimws(crf_site)))) #> [1] 5 ``` ::: Each site's label arrives in several spellings that differ in case and in leading or trailing spaces. `sort | uniq -c | cat -e` makes a trailing space visible as a space before the `$`. `readr` trims the spaces by default, so a count after `read_csv()` finds fewer spellings than the shell does; the shell is reporting what the file contains. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** What does `tail -n +2 labs.csv | cut -d, -f3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 1` print, read left to right? **Answer.** It drops the header of `labs.csv`, keeps the third comma-delimited field (the test code), sorts the values so that identical ones are adjacent, counts each distinct value (`uniq -c` needs the prior `sort`), sorts those counts in descending numeric order, and keeps the first line: the most frequent test and its count. It is the shell equivalent of `count(labs, test_code, sort = TRUE) |> slice(1)`. ::: ## Searching with grep and find {#sec-shell-search} `grep` searches file *contents*; `find` searches the file *tree*. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code} cd ../data/raw_data/hfhome grep -c '^"2433"' labs.csv find . -name '*.csv' -size +500k | sort #> 5 #> ./labs.csv #> ./medications.csv ``` ::: The first command counts the laboratory rows for patient `2433`, who appears in no other file: an orphan record that a join (@sec-joins) would silently drop or keep depending on its type. The second lists the CSV files larger than 500 kibibytes; `find` prints in directory order, which differs between systems, so the `sort` makes the output stable. The same two commands search a project's code (display-only): ```bash # every line that mentions the CRF export, with line numbers grep -rn "crf_export" R/ analysis/ # case-insensitive, in R scripts only grep -rni --include='*.R' "ntprobnp" . # every file over 100 MB (candidates to keep out of Git) find . -type f -size +100M ``` `grep` with a regular expression is the fastest way to answer 'where is this variable used?' across a project, and `find` is how you locate the large files that should never enter version control. ### Exercises 4. How many rows of `labs.csv` belong to patient `2433`? Which HF-HOME files are larger than 500 kibibytes? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} `grep -c '^"2433"' labs.csv` and `find . -name '*.csv' -size +500k`, run in the HF-HOME directory, as in the chunk above. The same answers in R: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} labs_raw <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "labs.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) sum(labs_raw$patient_id == "2433") #> [1] 5 csvs <- list.files(hf_dir, pattern = "[.]csv$", full.names = TRUE) basename(csvs[file.size(csvs) > 500 * 1024]) #> [1] "labs.csv" "medications.csv" ``` ::: The anchor `^` matters: without it, `grep -c '"2433"'` would also count any line in which `"2433"` appeared in another field. Here the identifier is the first field, so anchoring to the start of the line is exact. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** `grep -c 'Site E' crf_export.csv` returns a count. Is it the number of patients from Site E? **Answer.** No. It counts lines that contain the exact string `Site E`, and the export also spells the site in other cases (Exercise 3), which this pattern misses. `grep -ci 'site e'` is closer, but it would also match the string in any other field. The reliable count normalizes the one column first, as in Exercise 3, or is done in R after the same normalization. ::: ## Worked example: a script that checks the raw files {#sec-shell-worked} A pipeline you run by hand is a pipeline you will run differently next time. A shell script is a text file of commands with a `#!` line naming the interpreter; it records the steps, runs them identically every time, and is version-controlled with the analysis. The reproducibility argument of @sec-why applies to the shell as much as to R. The script below reports, for every CSV in a directory, the number of data rows and whether the file carries a BOM or carriage returns. It reads the files and writes nothing. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.bash .cell-code} #!/usr/bin/env bash # check-raw.sh: report rows, byte-order mark, and line endings set -euo pipefail dir="${1:-.}" printf '%-18s %6s %4s %5s\n' file rows bom crlf for f in "$dir"/*.csv; do rows=$(tail -n +2 "$f" | wc -l | tr -d ' ') first=$(head -c 3 "$f" | od -An -tx1 | tr -d ' \n') if [ "$first" = "efbbbf" ]; then bom=yes; else bom=no; fi if grep -q $'\r' "$f"; then crlf=yes; else crlf=no; fi printf '%-18s %6s %4s %5s\n' "$(basename "$f")" "$rows" \ "$bom" "$crlf" done ``` ::: Saved as `check-raw.sh`, it runs with `bash check-raw.sh ../data/raw_data/hfhome`, or, after `chmod +x check-raw.sh`, as `./check-raw.sh ../data/raw_data/hfhome`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ``` #> file rows bom crlf #> baseline.csv 2432 no no #> crf_export.csv 2432 yes yes #> demographics.csv 2432 no no #> labs.csv 23233 no no #> medications.csv 16927 no no #> outcomes.csv 2432 no no #> randomization.csv 2432 no no #> visits.csv 6317 no no ``` ::: Three lines make the script safe. `set -euo pipefail` stops it at the first failed command, at the first use of an unset variable, and at a failure anywhere in a pipeline, rather than letting it plow on; it is the single most valuable line in any script. Quoting every variable (`"$f"`, `"$dir"`) protects against paths that contain spaces. And `${1:-.}` gives the directory argument a default, so that `set -u` does not stop a run with no argument. A script that fetches the raw file in the first place needs one more guard (display-only, because it reaches the network): ```bash #!/usr/bin/env bash # fetch-raw.sh: download the extract into data/raw set -euo pipefail mkdir -p data/raw curl -fsSL "$1" -o data/raw/crf_export.csv ``` Without the `-f` flag, a server's '404 Not Found' page is saved as if it were the extract and the script carries on; with it, `curl` exits with an error and `set -e` stops the script. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Compare the script's row counts with R's for every file: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} script_rows <- read.table(text = check_out, header = TRUE) r_rows <- vapply(file.path(hf_dir, script_rows$file), \(p) { nrow(read_csv(p, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), na = character())) }, integer(1)) stopifnot(all(script_rows$rows == r_rows)) script_rows[script_rows$bom == "yes" | script_rows$crlf == "yes", ] #> file rows bom crlf #> 2 crf_export.csv 2432 yes yes ``` ::: The assertion passes, and only the CRF export carries a BOM or carriage returns. ::: ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} Ask a model or a coding agent for a script with the safety lines written into the request, and give an agent the dry-run rule as a standing instruction. > **Context.** I need a `bash` script that [describe the task: > takes a directory and moves every CSV older than 30 days into an > `archive/` subdirectory]. It will run on macOS and on Ubuntu. > > **Constraints.** Begin with `set -euo pipefail`; quote every > variable; take paths as arguments, never hard-coded. Never > delete, and never write into `data/raw/`. Every `rm`, `mv`, or > `>` that could overwrite a file must first run as > `echo rm ...` (or `echo mv ...`) behind a `--dry-run` flag that > is the default. > > **Criteria.** With no flags, the script prints the commands it > would run and changes nothing. Explain each line that changes a > file before the code. For a coding agent, put the rule in the project's instruction file (`AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`): 'Before any `rm`, `mv`, or redirection that overwrites a file, print the command with `echo` and wait for confirmation.' *Failure mode.* The script builds a deletion from a variable that is empty or unset (`rm -rf "$dir/"*` with `dir` empty is `rm -rf /*`), or redirects onto its own input. *Check.* Run the dry run on a copy in a `mktemp -d` directory, read every echoed command, then run it for real on the copy and compare `ls -R` before and after. A task description and file names are structure, not data (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ### Exercises 5. Extend `check-raw.sh` to print a fifth column: the number of columns in each file's header. Which HF-HOME file has the most columns? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} Add the count inside the loop and widen both `printf` lines: ```bash cols=$(head -n 1 "$f" | tr ',' '\n' | wc -l | tr -d ' ') ``` `tr` puts each header field on its own line and `wc -l` counts them; this is exact only because no HF-HOME header contains a quoted comma. The counts, from R: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} vapply(csvs, \(p) ncol(read_csv(p, n_max = 0, show_col_types = FALSE)), integer(1)) |> setNames(basename(csvs)) #> baseline.csv crf_export.csv demographics.csv labs.csv #> 6 8 11 5 #> medications.csv outcomes.csv randomization.csv visits.csv #> 3 8 6 5 ``` ::: `demographics.csv` has the most, because it carries the identifiers that the de-identification chapter removes. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A script without `set -euo pipefail` runs `curl -s "$1" -o data/raw/visits.csv` and then `Rscript analysis.R`. The URL has moved. What happens? **Answer.** Without `-f`, `curl` saves the server's error page as `visits.csv` and exits successfully; without `-e`, the script would have continued even if it had not. R then reads an HTML page as a CSV and, depending on the page, stops with a parse error or, worse, produces a one-column data frame that later steps summarize. With `curl -f` and `set -e`, the script stops at the download, with an error naming the URL. ::: ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 8: a bug that produces a plausible number is the expensive kind.** Look at the bytes with `od -c` and `cat -e` before trusting a count, and confirm every shell count in R. 2. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence.** Inspect raw files, never edit them in place; write repaired copies elsewhere, and never redirect onto a file you are reading. 3. **Habit 12: every model output is a hypothesis until verified.** Read a generated script before running it, and make every destructive command echo before it acts. ## Cumulative practice 6. *Cumulative (uses @sec-why).* A raw file is evidence only if you can show it has not changed. Write a checksum manifest for the HF-HOME CSV files with `md5sum *.csv > ../hfhome.md5` (on older macOS, `md5 -r` prints the same format), check it with `md5sum -c ../hfhome.md5`, and confirm one hash in R. What is the checksum of `crf_export.csv`? 7. *On your own work (no key).* Run `check-raw.sh` on the raw-data directory of a project of yours, and count the data rows of each file in R. Record any file whose counts disagree, and why. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} unname(tools::md5sum(crf_path)) #> [1] "874414afc4a04c50aab0fc29dea0da33" ``` ::: `md5sum -c` prints `OK` beside each file whose bytes still match; change one byte of a copy and it prints `FAILED`. The manifest is written outside the raw directory, so the directory holds only what you received, and the manifest belongs under version control (@sec-git-solo), so that its history shows when the evidence last changed. ::: ## Cheat sheet | Task | Command | |---|---| | Where am I; what is here | `pwd`; `ls -la` | | Move | `cd path`; `cd ..`; `cd -` | | First and last lines | `head -n 5 f`; `tail -n 5 f` | | Count data rows | `tail -n +2 f` \| `wc -l` | | See invisible bytes | `head -c 16 f` \| `od -c`; `head -n 2 f` \| `cat -e` | | Remove carriage returns, to a new file | `tr -d '\r' < f > ../derived/f` | | Count values of a column | `tail -n +2 f` \| `cut -d, -f2` \| `sort` \| `uniq -c` \| `sort -rn` | | Search contents | `grep -c 'pattern' f`; `grep -rn 'pattern' dir/` | | Search the tree | `find . -name '*.csv' -size +500k` | | Start a safe script | `#!/usr/bin/env bash`; `set -euo pipefail` | | Dry-run a deletion | `echo rm "$f"` | | Make a scratch directory | `tmp=$(mktemp -d)` | : The shell at a glance. {#tbl-shell-cheat-sheet} ## Further reading - The Software Carpentry lesson 'The Unix Shell' at `swcarpentry.github.io/shell-novice`, a hands-on introduction. - [@janssens2021dsatcl], the command line as a data-science tool, free online. - [@broman2019tools4rr], which covers the command line in the context of reproducible research. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-04b} 1. The pipe `|` sends the standard output of the command on its left to the standard input of the command on its right, so small tools compose into a pipeline. It is the direct ancestor of R's `|>`, which sends the value on its left as the first argument of the function on its right; both let you read a transformation left to right as a sequence of steps. 2. An absolute path names a location from the filesystem root and begins with `/` (or `~` for home); a relative path is interpreted from the current working directory. `.` is the current directory, `..` its parent, `~` your home directory, and `/` the root. 3. A hand-run sequence of steps is easy to run differently or incompletely next time, and it records nothing. A shell script runs the steps identically every time, can be version-controlled and reviewed, and documents the pipeline, which is the reproducibility argument of @sec-why applied to orchestration.
